measurement.happened:
The dominant story of this week in and around Iran is the sharp escalation of attacks in the Strait of Hormuz. On October 14, a container ship sank near the strait (CNBC, Wall Street Journal), and on October 15 two cargo ships were sunk as Iran ramped up attacks (CNN). By October 17, Iran's Revolutionary Guard confirmed that two additional tankers had been hit by mines (Reuters), and Iranian TV aired video of a tanker explosion (Al Jazeera). Both the US and Iran now claim effective control of the strait (Al Jazeera, October 17), and Iran has stepped up surveillance of the waterway while oil flows have crashed again (Al Jazeera, October 14). The US Navy destroyed an Iran-affiliated boat it said was conducting surveillance and targeting in the Gulf of Oman (Reuters, October 14) and a dhow suspected of being an Iranian command-and-control node (Al Jazeera, October 15). Three fishermen were injured in a drone incident off southern Iran (Reuters, October 14), and at least two security officials were killed near the critical port of Chabahar (Al Jazeera, October 14). In short, the strait has become the central battlefield of the war, and Iran is using it as a pressure valve ahead of the US midterm elections (CNN, October 15).

A second major theme is the US deliberating its next military options against Iran. President Trump said the US may need to strike Iran's Pickaxe Mountain nuclear site (Reuters, October 16) and mused about using the 'Mother of All Bombs' (Bloomberg, October 16; CNN, October 15; Reuters, October 15). Analysts and the Pentagon are weighing whether the MAB would actually hit Iran's deeply buried nuclear facilities (Bloomberg, October 16). Trump simultaneously ruled out using nuclear weapons or sending ground troops (CNBC, October 16), and one analyst called a major US strike before the midterms 'extremely unlikely' (CNBC, October 16). Amos Hochstein, a former US negotiator, said he has 'stopped understanding what the US strategy is' (CNBC, October 14). The Pentagon is also holding an internal report on an Iran school attack past the midterms (Bloomberg, October 15), suggesting a desire to manage the political fallout. Iran, for its part, boosted its air defenses in preparation for fresh US attacks (Bloomberg, October 16) and said it is 'counting the moments' until it can strike US warships (CNBC, October 14).

The Houthi-Saudi-Iran triangle intensified dramatically. Iran-aligned Houthis launched a deadly attack on the Yemeni presidential palace in Aden (CNN, October 15; TV5Monde, October 15), and Saudi Aramco's headquarters was hit in a Houthi attack (Bloomberg, October 14). A Saudi diplomat publicly accused Iran of encouraging the Houthi escalation (AP, October 15; TV5Monde, October 15), and Iran refuted the Saudi accusations the next day (TV5Monde, October 16). The Wall Street Journal reported on October 17 that Iran is giving the Houthis targeting data and intelligence for attacks on Saudi Arabia, confirming a close operational link. Reuters framed the Houthis as helping Iran turn Saudi Arabia into a new pressure point (October 15).

The economic fallout is severe and widening. Brent crude touched $110 on October 16 (CNBC), US crude was near $98 on October 15 (CNBC), and US inflation jumped to 3.7% driven in part by the Iran war (Financial Times, October 14). The IEA warned the diesel squeeze will last well into 2027 (CNBC, October 14). Oil majors face a $32 billion dilemma over war windfalls (FT, October 15). TotalEnergies flagged a quarterly profit surge driven by the war (Reuters, October 15). In the US, toy prices surged ahead of the holiday season (Reuters, October 15), retail price impacts are hitting households unevenly (AP, October 17), and Australians are cutting fuel purchases (Bloomberg, October 15). China is building a gas buffer for winter (Bloomberg, October 16). The UNDP chief sounded the alarm on growing poverty after the war shock (AFP, October 15). Iran's central bank governor dismissed claims of economic collapse amid the US blockade (Reuters, October 14), but US sanctions are leaving Iranians facing flight cancellations and soaring costs (Al Jazeera, October 16). The US issued fresh Iran-related sanctions (Reuters, October 15), Lebanon revoked the license of Iran's Bank Saderat under US pressure (Bloomberg, October 15), and Trump is weighing easing restrictions on Russian and Iranian 'shadow fleet' tankers (FT, October 15). Meanwhile, data shows Iran is still shipping some LPG and jet fuel despite the US blockade (Reuters, October 16).

US midterm politics are being shaped by the war. Iran war votes in Congress have become a focal point for campaign ad attacks (AP, October 17). In Alaska, candidates Sullivan and Peltola clashed over Iran and high prices in a Senate debate (AP, October 16). Democrats are hoping to flip Republican seats with veterans' help, fueled by anger over the war (AP, October 15). In Michigan, Trump's tariffs and the Iran war are becoming liabilities in the Senate race (CNBC, October 14). Iran itself is highlighting the cost of the war to American voters (Al Jazeera, October 16). Trump said the war will end 'soon as I want it to end' (CNN, October 15), but the timing is now entangled with the November elections. Russia, China, and Iran are also harnessing AI for US midterm disinformation (Bloomberg, October 14).

Inside Iran, political infighting is deepening as economic woes mount during the war (DW, October 14). The Tehran municipality was accused of 'overstepping' after launching welfare projects, suggesting internal power struggles (Al Jazeera, October 14). A young woman's brutal murder by her male relatives reignited the national debate over 'honor' killings and femicide (DW, October 16-17). Iran targeted Starlink as a 'tool of war' with hints of more internet curbs (Al Jazeera, October 14), and suspected Israeli online operations caused alarm in both Iran and Lebanon (Al Jazeera, October 14). Iran is also seeking 'harder targets' for attacks abroad, according to a UK warning (DW, October 14).

On the international espionage and intelligence front, a German court sentenced two men for plotting to kill the leader of the German Jewish community on behalf of Iran (Reuters, October 15; DW, October 15). A Norwegian teenager was sentenced to 20 years in prison for plotting a murder in the UK for an Iran-linked crime gang (AP, October 16; CNN, October 16; Bloomberg, October 16). The MI5 chief warned of threats to the UK from Russia, Iran, and AI (BBC, October 14). A London charity trustee was revealed to lead an Iranian propaganda body, per a tribunal hearing (FT, October 14). Russia's Lavrov and China's Wang discussed cooperation, Ukraine, and Iran at an Asia security meeting (Reuters, October 14). The G20 finance ministers and central bankers gathered amid the fallout from the Iran war (Al Jazeera, October 15).
measurement.expected:
Strait of Hormuz attacks: Almost certain that Iran will continue or even increase attacks on shipping in the strait over the coming week. The pattern this week was one of escalation (container ship, then two cargo ships, then two tankers hit by mines), and Iran has explicitly linked its timing to the US midterm calendar. Expect at least one or two more vessel incidents, possibly including a larger tanker or a US-flagged ship, before the November 3 elections. The US and Iran will continue to trade claims of control over the waterway. Confidence: almost certain.

Oil and energy prices: Almost certain that Brent crude will remain in the $100-$115 range, with possible spikes above $120 if a major tanker is hit or a US strike is announced. The IEA has already warned the diesel squeeze will persist into 2027, and China is actively building winter gas buffers. US retail fuel and goods prices will stay elevated, feeding directly into midterm campaign rhetoric. Confidence: almost certain.

US military posturing and rhetoric: Probable that Trump and senior officials will continue to float the 'Mother of All Bombs' and Pickaxe Mountain options in public, using them as bargaining chips and to signal resolve, while analysts and the Pentagon privately argue against a major strike before the midterms. Trump will likely rule out ground troops and nuclear weapons again. Expect at least one new round of US sanctions or a targeted strike on an Iranian naval or intelligence asset in the Gulf. Confidence: probable.

Houthi-Saudi escalation: Probable that the Houthis will launch at least one more significant attack on Saudi infrastructure (Aramco, Red Sea ports, or the presidential palace area in Aden), with Iran either tacitly endorsing or quietly refuting its role. Saudi Arabia will likely make another public accusation against Tehran. This axis is now a semi-independent front that Iran can use to pressure the US without directly hitting American soil. Confidence: probable.

Iran internal politics and society: Possible that the femicide/honor-killing debate will generate visible street protests or a wave of social media activism, especially given the economic strain. The political infighting between factions (municipality vs. central government, hardliners vs. pragmatics) may produce a visible cabinet reshuffle or a public spat on state TV. The Starlink/internet curbs issue could trigger a brief connectivity disruption or a new round of online censorship. Confidence: possible.

US midterm politics: Almost certain that the Iran war and its price tag will dominate at least two or three Senate and House debates in the week ahead. Democrats will push veterans' and blue-collar messaging on fuel and grocery prices. Republicans will defend the war as necessary but argue the US is 'winning.' Iran's own state media will run coordinated messaging aimed at American voters. Confidence: almost certain.

Diplomatic and back-channel activity: Possible that there will be quiet back-channel contacts between Washington and Tehran (via Oman, Qatar, or a European intermediary) to manage the Hormuz situation and avoid a full-blown exchange of fire before the midterms. A formal ceasefire or negotiation round is unlikely this week, but a de-escalation signal or a temporary pause in Hormuz attacks is possible if both sides want a calmer pre-election environment. Confidence: possible.

Less likely surprises: (1) A surprise US strike on Pickaxe Mountain or another nuclear site, which would be a major escalation but is considered 'extremely unlikely' by analysts before the midterms. (2) A visible Iranian protest movement or a brief internet shutdown in Tehran following the Starlink curbs. (3) A Houthi missile reaching a major Saudi oil refinery and causing a fire visible on satellite. (4) A new Iranian nuclear test or enrichment announcement timed to the news cycle.

Things I would not bet on: (1) A US ground invasion or deployment of a large expeditionary force to Iranian soil. (2) A formal ceasefire agreement or signed peace deal. (3) Iran accepting a new nuclear deal or significant concession on enrichment. (4) A change of government or succession crisis in Tehran. (5) The US using the 'Mother of All Bombs' in an actual strike (as opposed to threatening it). (6) A full US blockade of the Strait of Hormuz with carrier battle groups locking the waterway shut. (7) Iran launching a ballistic missile at a US carrier or a major European capital.
emoji_reasons: The Strait of Hormuz was the center of this week's story, with at least five ships hit or sunk and both the US and Iran claiming control of the waterway.

The war is actively escalating with the US weighing the 'Mother of All Bombs,' Iran boosting air defenses, and Houthi strikes hitting Saudi infrastructure, making armed conflict the defining backdrop.
Oil at $110, US inflation at 3.7%, new sanctions, and soaring consumer prices made the economic cost of the war the most felt consequence for ordinary people in the US, Iran, and beyond.
